title: Issue 1 Cover — The Impossible Flaw
summary: Founding Shattering cover. Sell the impossible flaw inside a civilization that still looks perfectly stable: the High Era corridor network is beautiful, green, synchronized, and trusted, while one duplicated vessel/arrival trace gives Liora the first visual proof that reality and the system no longer agree. This cover establishes Shattering's recurring masthead and trade dress without revealing the coming collapse.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed vertical cover. Liora is the human focal anchor in the lower-middle foreground at the edge of the BHA observation environment, small against the immense luminous High Era corridor network visible through live spatial visualization and distant traffic.

The network must look genuinely magnificent and dependable: elegant Cooperative/BHA architecture, green corridor lanes, disciplined civilian and freight movement, gold-white institutional accents, no damage, no panic.

Build the entire selling idea around one impossible visual fact: one vessel or arrival trace appears twice in the same corridor geometry, separated by a small but unmistakable temporal/spatial echo. It should be subtle enough to reward a second look but strong enough to remain visible at thumbnail size.

Liora is not posed heroically; she is caught noticing the contradiction. Her attention and the doubled trace should form one clean eyeline so the reader understands why the image matters without explanatory text.
The one-second cover read is: a perfect system contains one thing that cannot be true.
Do not show red network collapse, corridor tearing, the damping chamber, post-Break factions, the rescue vessel, or any mature Fleet ship/uniform/iconography.

Reserve the upper quarter as a clean integrated masthead field within the actual High Era visual environment, not a pasted banner. The art beneath the title must remain legible but visually quiet enough for premium trade dress.

title: Issue 2 Cover — Inherited Machinery
summary: Sell the central unease of Issue 2: the High Era lives comfortably atop systems older than its own understanding. The cover should make inherited infrastructure feel enormous, useful, and insufficiently understood while hinting that the answer may exist in forgotten layers beneath the polished civilization above.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed vertical cover built as one coherent architectural cutaway rather than a collage. Polished High Era civic/network infrastructure occupies the upper world; beneath it, older service strata and immense dormant harmonic machinery descend into darker structural depth.

Heska is the nearest human focal figure with Liora secondary, both small enough to emphasize inherited scale. Heska may hold or stand beside a Dawn Era schematic/provenance display, but its markings must remain non-legible visual geometry rather than environmental text.
One luminous green corridor line above should bow very slightly out of its expected path, visually connecting the healthy-looking civilization to the forgotten mass below.

The ancient machinery below should feel older, heavier, and only partly accessible. Suggest circular harmonic architecture and buried engineering, but do not clearly reveal the exact damping procedure or depict the dormant system as already found, opened, or activated.
The one-second cover read is: civilization is standing on a machine it inherited but no longer understands.

Avoid ruin-porn, mystical ancient-tech imagery, glowing prophecy symbols, mature Fleet aesthetics, or a literal split-screen between 'old' and 'new.' This is engineering history, not archaeology fantasy.
Keep the approved Issue 1 masthead geometry visually clean in the upper zone while allowing the cover art to descend dramatically through depth.

title: Issue 3 Cover — Two Instructions
summary: Sell the fatal pressure of Issue 3 without showing the failure: one ancient damping system is being asked to obey two incompatible ideas of stability. Liora's local engineering control and an official remote command path converge on the same machine, turning an institutional disagreement into immediate physical risk.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed vertical cover dominated by the circular architecture of the ancient damping apparatus. The machine should feel functional, dangerous, and engineered—not mystical.
Liora is the primary human focal figure at a local control position; Alan is secondary, physically close enough to share the operational problem rather than posed as a separate character portrait.

Visualize two instruction paths entering the same harmonic system: one locally coherent calibration geometry anchored to Liora's controls, and one clean official remote command path intruding from elsewhere in the BHA/Cooperative network. Keep both non-legible and diagrammatic.

The two control streams should begin orderly and become visibly incompatible only where they meet the apparatus. Do not depict the chamber exploding, Alan injured, emitters shearing apart, or corridor folding already underway.
The one-second cover read is: one machine is being told to do two different things.
Do not turn Lochran or Damian into looming villain faces. The conflict is institutional and procedural; the machine itself is where the contradiction becomes dangerous.
Preserve a clean upper masthead zone using the approved Issue 1 cover trade dress; the circular machine may frame or arc around that zone without obscuring the title.

title: Issue 4 Cover — The Road Breaks
summary: The season's spectacular cover. Sell the terrifying physical proposition of Issue 4: a road through impossible space stops agreeing with itself. A High Era vessel remains intact while its corridor geometry tears and a delayed duplicate of the ship appears where nothing should be.
settingText: Open High Era corridor space near a major convergence route during the first physically visible harmonic folding. The corridor is still recognizable as the same engineered green public infrastructure from earlier issues, but its geometry is beginning to lose agreement.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed cosmic cover with one High Era civilian/convoy vessel as the dominant physical object. The ship is not in combat and is not exploding.

The luminous green corridor lane bends, splits, and slips out of registration around the vessel. A delayed second silhouette/echo of the same ship hangs beside or behind it in impossible open space, clearly the same hull displaced by harmonic folding rather than a second craft.
Use the corridor itself as the dramatic architecture: green route geometry fractures into offset ribbons and anchor points while the surrounding void remains stark and clean.
The vessel's real silhouette and its displaced echo must remain readable at thumbnail size. Avoid filling the image with many ships, debris, weapons, or unrelated disaster effects.
The one-second cover read is: the road itself has broken.
Do not show the final five nodes dying, the full network gone, the post-Break world, rescue-cluster success, or any mature Shard/Fleet visual language.
The approved masthead should sit against a deliberately calmer region of space/corridor glow so the title remains crisp despite the issue's largest-scale spectacle.

title: Issue 5 Cover — Three Ways to Survive
summary: Sell the birth of future political traditions as practical behavior, not as a faction lineup. After the Break, one damaged piece of shared infrastructure is being made usable through three different habits: improvised repair, hand-verified route trust, and accountable inspection. The shared safety mark sits at the center before anyone agrees what it will eventually mean.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed post-Break cover centered on one battered but vital shared infrastructure threshold: a doorway, relay housing, structural support, or service junction that people actually need to keep using.
The ancestral safety sigil is the visual center, newly applied or being completed on the shared surface. It must read as one common mark, not three mature faction emblems.

Around that same center, show three practical systems converging without arranging the characters as a team pose: Ruben's improvised brace/repair hardware physically keeps the structure working; Ava's hand-verified route tokens or map-thread logic identifies who can safely use or reach it; Iskara's inspection/accountability marks establish what someone is willing to certify.
Faces may be visible but should remain subordinate to the work. Hands, tools, route material, and the shared mark carry the issue's argument.
Use restrained ancestral hints of later visual traditions only through materials and behavior. Do not color-code the image into mature Core/Fleet blue-gold-white, Verge green, and Shard red teams.
The one-second cover read is: three different ways of keeping people alive are becoming three different ideas of order.
Do not show the later prototype rescue vessel, a completed mature faction system, a solved political settlement, or Liora's final treatise state.
Keep a clean masthead zone consistent with Issue 1 while allowing the post-Break palette to be rougher, more material, and less polished than the High Era covers.

title: Issue 6 Cover — Future on the Gantry
summary: Sell the finale as a future being assembled before its politics are settled. The prototype multiworld rescue vessel is nearly ready on the gantry, built from mixed post-Break practices and carrying the shared ancestral safety sigil, while the command position remains visibly unresolved. The ship is consequential precisely because it is not yet the mature Fleet.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed finale cover dominated by the prototype rescue vessel on its service gantry immediately beside the repurposed Resolve Circle/logistics space. The vessel is nearly ready but visibly improvised, practical, and pre-Fleet.

Mixed crews and equipment feed the ship from different post-Break practices: patched engineering hardware, hand-verified route material, annotated standards, and shared relief supplies. These contributions should visually converge on the vessel rather than become separate faction zones.
Place the shared ancestral safety sigil prominently on the vessel as a practical common mark. It must not yet look like a finished mature Fleet/Crown/Verge/Shard emblem.

Make the unresolved command question visible without environmental text: an unoccupied captain/command position, open command station, or deliberately empty central place in the boarding/preflight composition. Do not render a readable blank roster or label.

Iskara, Ruben, and Ava may appear as small working figures in different operational roles; do not pose them heroically in front of the ship. Liora is not physically present at the gantry and must not be inserted for symbolic convenience.
The one-second cover read is: the future is ready to move before anyone has finished deciding what it is.
Do not show the vessel already launched, the final escort formation, mature Rex Fleet ships or uniforms, the future faction order, or the final historical interpretation.
Use the approved Issue 1 masthead/trade-dress system unchanged at its proper scope, while letting the finale's ship silhouette and gantry lighting create the most forward-looking cover of the run.
